newsitem.title: GERMANY: Weather plays havoc with Franco-German talks.
newsitem.headline: Weather plays havoc with Franco-German talks.

text.p: Foggy weather complicated regular talks of the Franco-German econonic council on Tuesday, forcing German and French officials to find an impromptu meeting place in the Stuttgart airport VIP lounge.
Talks were scheduled to begin at 0800 GMT in the Bavarian town of Kempten. But fog at the nearby Memmingen airport prevented French and German officials from arriving on time.
Planes were diverted to Stuttgart and the talks began there in an airport lounge once all the officials had arrived, a spokeswoman for the German finance ministry said.

But the talks between German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis and Bank of France President Jean-Claude Trichet were expected to be moved to Kempten at about 0900 GMT.
"Once they were all there, they decided it would make sense to start the discussions immediately," she said. "We hope they will be here in about an hour."
It was not yet clear whether a news conference planned for 1130 GMT in Kempten would begin on time.

The meeting, sandwiched between critical budget talks in Bonn and Paris this week, fall three days ahead of an informal meeting of European Union finance officials in Dublin which will address key aspects of the single currency project.

Germany and France, the two countries unanimously regarded as indispensible founder members of the planned European currency, will agree on their joint position for the Dublin talks in the framework of broader economic discussions.

Such Franco-German meetings regularly end with an upbeat summary of each country's growth prospects, optimism that jobless figures will fall and above all a reaffirmation of joint determination to make the single currency a success.
One source familiar with Bonn's position on European Economic and Monetary Union said there were unlikely to be any major new European initiatives emerging from Kempten.
He dismissed financial market talk of a stronger currency link between the French franc and the German mark as unrealistic.

The Maastricht Treaty -- which sets goals on interest and exchange rates, inflation and public budgets -- calls for Euro nations to have deficits of no more than three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997.

Germany, the self-appointed guardian of Europe's fiscal discipline, is already aiming well below that level, and will hope to inspire France's financial leaders with the confidence to adopt hardline measures in the face of public protest.
Waigel has parliamentary approval for three key bills in his pocket, giving him a confidence boost to implement the austerity budget.

But the French government, which is due to present its budget on Wednesday, is already showing signs of flagging in its determination to push such measures through, harried by negative public opinion and the threat of widespread strikes.

The 1997 French budget, which aims to bring the total public deficit to within three percent of GDP from a targeted four percent this year, contains substantial spending cuts, but is much less harsh than many had expected.
Instead, one-off revenue, including a transfer of 37 billion francs ($7.17 billion) to cover France Telecom pensions, will be used to help it reach the three percent goal.
Tietmeyer last week indirectly criticised such window-dressing, making clear that fiscal stability was not simply a question of juggling figures.
